item.title: China services PMI slows to 50.8 in October as price cuts meet rising costs
item.description:
The data adds to the picture of a Chinese economy still growing but struggling with weak pricing power, which helps explain why authorities are leaning on targeted support such as this week’s expanded buyback lending. Falling selling prices alongside rising costs point to margin pressure for listed service companies, which may limit any equity bounce from the support measures. Firms specifically cited oil among rising input costs, a sign that higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict are filtering into China’s economy even as companies cannot pass them on. For the Australian dollar and commodities, the slightly firmer manufacturing output is a modest offset, but the softer services reading gives little reason to expect a stronger demand impulse from China.

--- Chinese service firms are still finding customers and hiring staff, but they are cutting prices to do it while their own costs climb, a squeeze that shows up in profits before it shows up in growth.

Summary:

  • The RatingDog China General Services PMI fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6, the slowest growth in three months
  • New business rose at a solid pace, and new export orders grew for a sixth month
  • Employment rose for a sixth month at a faster pace, and backlogs fell for the first time in a year, helped by AI efficiencies
  • Selling prices fell for a second month, while input costs rose at the fastest pace in five months on labour, raw material and oil costs
  • Business confidence slipped to a three-month low
  • The composite PMI fell to 52.0 from 52.4, despite faster manufacturing output growth

China’s services sector kept growing in October but at a slower pace, a private survey showed on Wednesday. Firms cut prices to win business even though their own costs rose at the fastest rate in five months.

The RatingDog China General Services PMI, compiled by S&P Global, fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6 in September. The reading stayed above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction, but it showed the slowest growth in activity in three months. Firms pointed to operational constraints as a factor behind the slowdown.

Demand held up better than the headline suggests. New business continued to rise at a solid pace, little changed from September, extending a run of growth that began in January 2023. Firms credited wider customer bases and successful promotional efforts. New export orders rose for a sixth straight month, the longest stretch since 2024, though growth eased and was marginal.

Hiring picked up. Employment rose for a sixth month, and at a faster pace than in September, as firms took on both full- and part-time staff. The extra workers, along with what firms described as efficiency gains from AI, helped reduce backlogs of work for the first time in a year.

Pricing remains the main concern. Average selling prices fell for a second month as firms discounted to cope with fierce competition, although the pace of discounting eased from September. At the same time, input cost inflation hit a five-month high, driven by higher labour, raw material and oil costs, with some firms also citing social security payments. That combination points to pressure on profit margins.

Business confidence stayed positive but slipped to a three-month low, as firms worried about rising costs and competition.

A separate composite index, which combines manufacturing and services, fell to 52.0 from 52.4, the slowest rise in private sector output in three months. Faster growth in manufacturing output was not enough to offset the softer services expansion.

RatingDog founder Yao Yu said that steady new business and stronger hiring underpinned growth at the start of the fourth quarter, but that renewed discounting and rising costs were weighing on profitability. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Sell tech, sell USD and other signals from the massive blue wave that's unfolding
item.description:
The US dollar is selling off as the election results roll in and they show a total repudation of Republican policies.

Fox News is talking about the Iran war as a disaster at the ballot box and in terms of affordability, which was clearly on the ballot. Tariffs aren't far behind. 

Still, it's tough to price in a reversal in Iran or on tariffs with Trump in office for another two years. What is driving markets and could swing is data centers and AI. Democrats took an anti-AI stance or at least something slower than the full-throttle roll out now. In Texas and Ohio in particular, data centers became a huge issue and it looks like the pro-data center candidates will lose the Governorship. 

Moreover, tech companies dove into bed with Trump ahead of the last election and most have gotten more-deeply involved since, as they were given to move fast and break things. Now, Democrats might look for some retribution for the massive checks they wrote to Republicans, via regulation, fines and investigations. That's why the Nasdaq is down 1.5% at the moment.

Moreover, the AI trade is vulnerable already and this could tip it further. In terms of FX, the dollar is increasingly an AI-investment trade. If we see a reversal of the flows into AI, that means the money will flow out of USD. We've seen this dynamic unfolding in the past two months with an increasingly-tight correlation. 

I worry there could be some second and third order effects if Trump attacks Iran in a fit, or grows less predictable. For now, I think the market is sending the right signals: Sell tech, sell USD.

To give you a sense of how big of an upset this is -- even compared to expectations -- is that Lindsay Graham's seat looks lost. The odds of that in October were just 14%.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: China buyback loan applications top 200bn yuan as PBOC steps up stock support
item.description:
The modest early gains suggest the measures are steadying sentiment rather than sparking a rebound, consistent with the scheme’s role as a backstop. The benefit is likely to be greatest for large, cash-rich companies with high dividend yields, such as state-owned banks and energy firms, which can borrow cheaply to buy back shares. The tool does little directly for the tech and AI names behind October’s sell-off, so Hong Kong-listed tech remains exposed to AI earnings concerns. For the Australian dollar and iron ore, stabilising Chinese equities offer marginal support, but property and consumption data remain the bigger drivers.

---

Beijing is not buying stocks itself, but it is making it very cheap for companies and their owners to do so, and demand for that money is climbing fast.

Summary:

  • Applications for the PBOC’s share buyback and stake-increase relending scheme have topped 200bn yuan, about $30bn
  • The PBOC said it has intensified the policy to keep capital markets stable
  • This week it cut the facility rate to 1% from 1.25%, made the tool permanent and widened eligibility
  • A separate 100bn yuan asset swap facility for brokers, fund managers and insurers began on Tuesday
  • The CSI 300 fell 8.5% in October, its worst month in a decade, on doubts over AI and tech spending
  • Shanghai stocks edged higher in early trade

Applications for China’s central bank-backed share buyback loans have topped 200bn yuan, or about $30bn, the People’s Bank of China said on Wednesday, according to Reuters. Authorities are stepping up efforts to steady a stock market that has suffered its worst month in a decade. Mainland shares edged higher in early trade, with the Shanghai Composite up about 0.2% at around 3,610 shortly after the open.

The PBOC said it had intensified its share repurchase and shareholding relending policies to keep capital markets stable. The update follows a meeting on Monday at which the central bank and financial and securities regulators met major banks to discuss how to improve the scheme.

So how does it work? The facility, launched in October 2024 with a quota of 300bn yuan, is a form of targeted cheap funding. Commercial banks lend to listed companies so they can buy back their own shares, and to major shareholders so they can raise their stakes. The PBOC then supplies low-cost funding to the banks to cover those loans, which is what relending means. The central bank does not buy shares itself. Instead, it lowers the cost for companies and their main owners to do so.

The aim is to put a floor under prices. Buybacks reduce the number of shares in circulation and signal that insiders see value at current levels. Because the loans are cheap, a company can borrow to buy its own stock when its dividend yield exceeds the cost of borrowing, which turns falling prices into an incentive to buy.

Authorities made the scheme more generous this week. On Monday, the PBOC cut the interest rate it charges banks under the facility to 1% from 1.25%, made the tool a permanent part of its policy kit and widened the range of eligible companies. It also opened a separate asset swap facility of about 100bn yuan. That facility lets brokers, fund managers and insurers swap assets for more liquid securities, which they can use to raise cash to buy shares.

The push comes after a sharp sell-off. The CSI 300 index of major mainland stocks fell 8.5% in October and entered a bear market on 20 October, hit by doubts over whether Chinese AI and technology companies will earn back their heavy spending. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-linked firms make up about 42% of the market value of Chinese shares listed on the mainland and in Hong Kong.

Tools like this have limits. Buybacks support prices but do not fix the underlying problems weighing on Chinese stocks, including weak consumption and a long property downturn. Repurchased shares that are not cancelled can also be sold back into the market later, and borrowing to buy stock adds to corporate debt. The scheme works best as a backstop that slows selling, rather than as a trigger for a lasting rally. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: It's no longer early, this election is looking like a disaster for Republicans
item.description:
It's no longer early as US votes roll in.

There is a highly statistically significant number of districts reporting now and some of them reporting completely. The numbers are showing a 10-35 point swing towards Democrats. If even the bottom of that holds, it's a huge swing towards Democrats.

For illustration, betting odds now have Democrats winning the Texas Governorship and Senate seat, with Talarico beating Paxton at 95%. In the closely-watched early numbers in KY-06 and IN-05 the numbers are unmistakable and show Democrats upsetting Republicans in both. Florida hasn't been as much of a landslide but it has shown a shift to Democrats of around 10 points from 2024.

Another huge upset brewing is in South Carolina, where Lindsay Graham's sister was running for his seat after his death. Odds now have her narrowly losing the seat, which would hand it to Democrats for the next 6 years. 

On Kalshi, Democrat control of the Senate is now at 96.8%.

It seems that all that's left to do is tally the margin of victory.

In terms of markets, I would be careful with tech because anti data-centers was a strong campaign message and anti-AI in general. The tech right got into bed with Trump and now there might be a price to pay. That's particularly notable in Texas, where there are a huge amount of data centers planned. Shares of Tesla are down 3% overnight and I think that's an interesting spot to watch if the Democrat wins the Governorship. 

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stock futures slip on Globex as early midterm results point to Democratic gains
item.description:
The reaction is likely to spill into Asian trade, where regional equities tend to follow US futures in the absence of a local catalyst. The dollar and Treasuries are worth watching for signs of whether markets see a Democratic Congress as reducing fiscal stimulus expectations, which would tend to support bonds. Oil could be sensitive to any shift in expectations for Iran policy, with congressional constraints on military action potentially easing the geopolitical risk premium. Volatility measures may stay elevated until the balance of power in both chambers is confirmed.

---

Earlier:

  • The very early results in Kentucky show a massive swing towards Democrats

---

Futures are trading the early midterm returns before the votes are counted, betting that a divided Washington means less policy support and more political noise.

Summary:

  • US stock index futures traded lower on Globex as early midterm results pointed to Democratic gains
  • No call has yet been made on control of the House or Senate
  • Narratives include a stalled legislative agenda, renewed fiscal standoffs and greater oversight of the administration
  • Technology, pharma, financials, energy and defence could face sector-specific pressure
  • Gridlock has historically been seen as benign for stocks, and markets have often rallied after midterms
  • Thin overnight liquidity means early moves may not last

US stock index futures traded lower on Globex as early results from Tuesday’s midterm elections pointed to Democratic gains. Traders are weighing the prospect that the party could take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

No call has yet been made on the balance of power in either chamber, and counting is continuing. The moves in futures reflect early positioning in thin overnight trade rather than a settled verdict on the result.

Several explanations are circulating for the weakness. The most direct is that a Democratic Congress would end the White House’s ability to pass its agenda through the legislature. Further tax cuts, deregulation and other fiscal measures that some investors had built into earnings expectations would become much harder to deliver.

Divided government would also bring back the risk of standoffs over government funding and the debt ceiling, which have produced bouts of volatility in past cycles. A Democratic House would gain subpoena power and control of committees, raising the prospect of investigations into the administration and adding to political uncertainty.

Some of the pressure may show up at the sector level. Technology and AI companies could face more scrutiny through congressional hearings, drugmakers may see renewed pressure on pricing, and banks and crypto firms may find deregulation slows. Energy and defence stocks could also be sensitive to any congressional effort to limit military action against Iran or to challenge the administration’s tariff powers.

There are reasons for caution about reading too much into the early moves. Market wisdom has long held that gridlock can be positive for stocks because it limits major policy shifts. US equities have also historically tended to perform well in the months after midterm elections, once uncertainty clears. Overnight liquidity is thin, and other factors, including the Iran stand-off and concerns about AI valuations, have weighed on sentiment this week.

The cash market open, and confirmation of control in each chamber, will give a clearer read on whether the selling extends or fades.

Team Trump not having a good evening so far

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Recap: New Zealand jobless rate hits 11-year high, kiwi slips as RBNZ hike bets fade
item.description:
The steady drift lower in the kiwi since the release suggests traders are pricing out some of the chance of a December hike rather than reacting to a one-off headline. The fall in two-year swaps supports that reading. With the RBA still leaning hawkish, the widening policy gap leaves NZD/AUD vulnerable to further weakness. The election is the next risk: a Labour-led win would bring the prospect of a dual mandate, which markets would likely read as tilting the RBNZ toward easier policy over time. Inflation expectations surveys later this month are the next test of whether the RBNZ’s hawks can still make their case.

---

Earlier:

  • NZ Q3 Unemployment rate 5.7% (expected 5.5%, prior 5.6%)

---

New Zealand’s jobs data missed on every measure, handing the RBNZ a reason to stay on hold and the opposition a fresh line of attack days before the vote.

Summary:

  • Unemployment rose to 5.7% in Q3, the highest since 2015, against expectations of 5.5% from both economists and the RBNZ
  • Employment fell 0.1% and participation slipped to 70.4%
  • Private sector wage growth slowed to 0.4% in the quarter and 2.0% on the year
  • The kiwi dipped, steadied around $0.56 and has drifted lower since, while two-year swaps fell about 6bp
  • Labour called the data a verdict on the government, while the finance minister urged voters to stick with its plan
  • Labour has pledged to restore a dual mandate for the RBNZ if elected on Saturday

New Zealand’s unemployment rate climbed to an 11-year high in the third quarter, data released earlier on Wednesday showed. The New Zealand dollar has traded lower since, as markets weigh the outlook for interest rates and Saturday’s general election.

To recap, the jobless rate rose to 5.7% in the three months to September, the highest since 2015, according to Statistics New Zealand. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 5.5%, as had the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Employment fell 0.1% from the previous quarter, against forecasts of a 0.4% rise, and the participation rate slipped to 70.4%, below the 70.7% expected.

Wage growth also slowed. Private sector labour costs excluding overtime rose 0.4% in the quarter, down from 0.7% in the previous three months, taking annual growth to 2.0% from 2.1%.

The figures land in the final days of a tight election campaign, Reuters reported, with an Ipsos poll this week showing inflation and the cost of living as voters’ top concern. Labour’s finance spokesperson, Barbara Edmonds, said the data was a damning judgement on Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s handling of the economy. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the numbers reflected the effect of uncertainty and showed the need to stay with the government’s plan, which she said was rebuilding the economy.

Markets read the data as reducing pressure on the central bank to resume rate rises. The kiwi dipped on the release before steadying around $0.56, Reuters reported, and has since drifted lower. Two-year swap rates fell about 6 basis points to around 3.78%.

The RBNZ surprised markets last week by holding its official cash rate at 2.75%. It said it wanted time to judge the effect of two earlier hikes, while signalling further increases were still likely. Economists at one local bank said the weakening labour market made that decision look increasingly justified, and suggested further hikes may not be needed if the trend continued.

The election adds a further policy question. Labour has pledged to return the RBNZ to a dual mandate covering both price stability and maximum sustainable employment, rather than its current single focus on inflation. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tesla misled South Korean buyers over Full Self-Driving, consumer group alleges
item.description:
The direct financial hit to Tesla is likely small, but the case adds to regulatory and reputational risk around Full Self-Driving, a product central to the company’s valuation story. A cease-and-desist order or fines in a fast-growing market would be a setback. Refund claims would be a bigger issue if they spread to other countries selling China-built cars. The dispute also highlights how much Tesla’s international software revenue depends on certification regimes it does not control, which matters as it pushes for approval in Europe. Investors will watch whether the regulator acts quickly and whether similar complaints emerge elsewhere.

---

Tesla’s South Korean boom was built on China-made cars, and a consumer group says the company sold their owners self-driving software they could never legally switch on.

Summary:

  • A consumer group plans to file a complaint on Thursday alleging Tesla misled South Korean buyers over Full Self-Driving, Reuters reported
  • Only about 20% of Teslas registered in South Korea, those made in the US, can legally use the software
  • 99% of new Teslas sold in South Korea last year were China-made and ineligible
  • Tesla charged about 9 million won (around $6,700) for the software before moving to a monthly subscription in August
  • The group seeks a cease-and-desist order, fines and a referral to state investigators
  • The regulator already opened a probe into Tesla’s advertising earlier this year

A consumer advocacy group alleges that Tesla misled tens of thousands of South Korean customers by marketing its Full Self-Driving software, even though the company knew the software could not legally be used in most of its cars sold there. The group plans to file a complaint on Thursday, Reuters reported.

According to Reuters, which has seen the previously unreported complaint, Citizens United for Consumer Sovereignty will ask the Korea Fair Trade Commission to issue a temporary cease-and-desist order on marketing the software for ineligible vehicles. It will also seek administrative fines and a referral to state investigators. Tesla did not respond to requests for comment.

At the centre of the dispute is where the cars are built. Tesla Korea’s country manager told a parliamentary hearing last month that the software can be used on only about 20% of Tesla vehicles registered in South Korea. Those are the US-built cars, which meet American safety standards recognised under a free trade agreement. Most Teslas sold in the country are made in China, where no such arrangement exists.

Tesla has sold more than 170,000 Shanghai-built vehicles in South Korea since 2023, according to company data submitted to the National Assembly. Last year, 99% of new Teslas sold in the country could not legally use the software. For years, Tesla charged customers a one-off payment of about 9 million won, or roughly $6,700, before switching to a monthly subscription of about 150,000 won in August.

The complaint alleges Tesla promoted the feature as coming soon and released a demonstration video filmed in South Korea, without clearly disclosing that only a small fraction of its cars could use it. The group’s automotive lead said Tesla had earned substantial revenue from selling a costly system that many buyers could not use at all.

Regulatory scrutiny was already under way. A commission official said it opened a probe into Tesla’s advertising of the software earlier this year and has received written responses from the company. The transport ministry has said the software does not meet local safety rules, including a requirement for drivers to keep their hands on the wheel. Tesla applied for certification of China-made vehicles only in late October.

The case comes as Tesla’s sales in South Korea surge. It overtook BMW this year as the country’s top imported car brand.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6811 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
Yesterday the PNoC made moves to slow the yuan appreciation:

  • China’s PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD

---

The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

Pan Gongsheng, Governor of the People's Bank of China

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: India gold demand seen at six-year low in 2026 as high prices and weak monsoon bite
item.description:
Weak Indian buying removes an important source of physical support for gold, leaving prices more reliant on central bank purchases and fund inflows. Lower imports would ease pressure on India’s trade deficit and offer modest support to the rupee, though the reported rise in unofficial inflows means official import data may understate actual demand. The Diwali and wedding season is the near-term test: a muted festival response would confirm that current prices have moved beyond what Indian households will pay. For the wider gold market, it reinforces a pattern of strong official demand alongside a retreat by price-sensitive consumers.

---

Earlier:

  • Central bank gold buying jumps 42% in Q3 as high prices hit jewellery demand, WGC says

---

The world’s second-biggest gold buyer is pulling back, priced out by gold’s rally and squeezed by a failed monsoon, just as its key buying season begins.

Summary:

  • The WGC expects India’s 2026 gold demand to fall to around 650 tons, the lowest since 2020
  • September-quarter demand fell 29% to around 160 tons, with jewellery down 20% and investment down 40%
  • Rising living costs since the Iran war and the weakest monsoon in more than a decade are weighing on rural buying
  • Rural areas account for more than half of India’s gold demand
  • Festival and wedding demand should lift the December quarter, but high prices are expected to cap the recovery
  • Official imports fell partly due to more unofficial inflows after higher import duties

India’s gold demand is expected to fall to a six-year low in 2026, as elevated prices weigh on jewellery buying and investment demand weakens, the World Gold Council said on Tuesday, according to Reuters.

The industry body expects total demand in the world’s second-largest gold consumer to fall to around 650 metric tons this year. That would be the lowest since 2020, when pandemic lockdowns forced jewellery shops to close. Sachin Jain, chief executive of the council’s Indian operations, told Reuters that weaker jewellery sales over the first nine months of the year would drag down the annual total.

Demand fell 29% from a year earlier to around 160 tons in the September quarter, Jain said. Jewellery purchases dropped 20%, while investment demand fell 40%.

The figures show high prices hitting Indian buyers harder than the global market. The council’s global report, also released on Tuesday, showed worldwide demand roughly flat on the year in the third quarter, with strong central bank buying offsetting weaker jewellery and retail investment.

Indian households are also facing rising living costs following the Iran war, and the weather has added to the strain. The 2026 monsoon delivered its lowest rainfall in more than a decade, cutting farm output and incomes in rural areas. Those areas account for more than half of the country’s gold demand, and jewellery there serves as a traditional store of wealth.

Jain said demand should pick up in the December quarter, when festivals and the wedding season typically lift purchases. Diwali, when buying gold is considered auspicious, falls in early November. However, the council said high prices and the weak rural economy were likely to limit any recovery.

India’s official gold imports also fell in the September quarter. Jain attributed part of the decline to a rise in unofficial inflows after the government raised import duties on gold earlier this year. That suggests official data may understate how much gold is entering the country. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The very early results in Kentucky show a massive swing towards Democrats
item.description:
I highlighted KY-06 as an early district to watch as a barometer of today's vote and now some real results are crossing and betting markets are moving.

In Anderson County, the numbers show the Republican Alvarado leading by 19 percentage points. That's good, right? No, it's not because in the prior three House elections, the Republican won that county +48, +54 and +54. So that's around a 35-points swing towards the Democrat candidate with 49% of votes counted.

In Montgomery County on the opposite side of the district, 43% of votes are counted and the patter is similar. It shows Alvarado up 16 points but that compares to +53 in the prior election, +54 in 2022 and +43 in 2020.

In Jessamine County, with 27% of the vote, Dumbo leads +0.9% and that compares to R+46.3% in 2024, a huge swing. That's a smaller percentage of the vote but the raw number is triple the size of the other two counties that have reported.

That looks like a Democratic landslide and prediction markets appear to endorse it. 

There has also been a notable move towards Democrats winning the Senate at 86% compared to 73% earlier today.

For Kentucky, there is an important caveat here. Nearly all Kentucky counties are expected to report early and absentee votes in their first update, according to the Associated Press. Those numbers are likely from early and mail-in voters, which skew Democrat. 

Update: Likely the most-significant data point yet is in. 95% of votes are in for Powell County in KY-06 and that's a 28.7 pt swing to Dems vs 2024 and 27 pts vs 2022. With the high % counted, it can't be a mail-in skew.

Update 2: Now we have 89-92% of votes counted in Montgomery, Anderson and Bourbon Counties. As the later votse come in, we've seen a 3-5 point swing towards the Republicans but that's still a massive underperformance compared to 2024. In those counties, the movement is Dem +32.4, +32.3 and +37.4 points. Dumbo is now pricing at 95%.

If that translates nationally, it will be a LANDSLIDE.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump says no immediate plan to strike Iran as Netanyahu hints at attack this week
item.description:
Trump’s remarks could take some heat out of crude, as they reduce the near-term chance of a fresh US-led escalation that markets had begun to price after Netanyahu’s hints. Any relief is likely to be limited, because oil’s risk premium rests on the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks, the US blockade of Iranian ports and Monday’s limited US strikes keep supply risk live. The bigger swing factor for oil is whether the Qatari-mediated talks produce a Hormuz deal, which would ease shipping risk far more than any single comment from Washington. A divergence between Trump and Netanyahu also leaves open the risk of Israeli action without full US backing, which would likely push prices sharply higher.

If Trump is planning strikes he is doing well to keep his mouth shut about it. 

--

Trump is in no hurry to escalate with Iran, but Netanyahu is, and oil markets will be watching which of them sets the timetable.

Summary:

  • Trump said the US has no immediate plan to strike Iran, according to the FT
  • He said the US appeared to be getting everything it wanted from the stand-off
  • Asked about Netanyahu’s hints of an attack this week, he said the US was ready but there may be no need
  • Netanyahu has been pressing for new strikes after the US midterms, AP reported
  • US forces carried out limited, unannounced strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Monday
  • Qatari-mediated talks on a Hormuz and port blockade framework continue this week

US President Donald Trump said the United States has no immediate plan to strike Iran, according to the Financial Times. He signalled he is comfortable with the current stand-off even as Israel’s prime minister hints at military action later this week.

Trump said Washington appeared to be getting everything it wanted from the situation. He was asked about strong suggestions from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that an attack could come within days. Trump replied that the US was fully ready to act if needed, but that there might be no reason to do so.

The comments point to a gap between Washington and Israel. Netanyahu has been pressing Trump to launch a new wave of strikes after the US midterm elections, which take place on Tuesday, according to officials cited by the Associated Press. Those officials suggested a return to full-scale war could help Netanyahu rebuild a governing coalition after he and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Trump did not commit to strikes during a call with Netanyahu at the weekend.

Trump’s remarks do not mean US military activity has stopped. US forces carried out limited strikes on Monday against Iranians who had fired missiles at American forces in the Strait of Hormuz, the AP reported. Iranian state media reported explosions on islands in the strait and near the port of Bandar Abbas. The US did not publicly announce the operation.

Diplomacy is also continuing. Qatari mediators held two rounds of talks with Iranian officials last week, with more planned this week. A framework under discussion would see Iran halt attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran is seeking guarantees that Washington would honour any agreement.

The conflict began on 28 February, when US and Israeli strikes killed Iran’s then supreme leader. His successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, has reportedly ordered forces to respond to any threat without geographic limits. That stance leaves the risk of escalation high whatever Washington’s current intentions.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BMW issues second profit warning, says car business could slip into operating loss
item.description:
The warning adds pressure on European auto stocks heading into Frankfurt’s open, with Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen exposed to the same China weakness. The cut is partly self-inflicted, through faster restructuring and production ramp-up costs, so investors may treat it as less severe than a pure demand shock. The intact cash flow target supports that reading. Still, a margin range that includes a loss is a striking signal for a premium carmaker, and it could reinforce caution on the sector’s China exposure. Wednesday’s results will decide whether the selloff deepens or stabilises.

--- BMW’s car business could now lose money this year, though part of the damage comes from cutting jobs faster and building popular new models, not just from China.

Summary:

  • BMW cut its 2026 automotive operating margin forecast to minus 0.5% to plus 0.5%, from 1% to 3% set in June
  • It is the company’s second profit warning this year
  • Faster job cuts will bring larger severance costs in Q4, and management roles will be reduced more quickly
  • Strong demand for Neue Klasse models requires costly extra shifts
  • Deliveries are now expected to fall more steeply than planned, while the automotive free cash flow target of above €2.5bn holds
  • BMW reports Q3 results on Wednesday

BMW issued its second profit warning of the year on Tuesday, cutting its forecast for the core margin at its car business to a range that includes the possibility of an operating loss. Faster job cuts are adding to costs, and demand in China remains weak.

The Munich-based carmaker now expects its automotive operating margin to come in between minus 0.5% and plus 0.5% in 2026. In June it had forecast a range of 1% to 3%, which was itself a downgrade from its outlook at the start of the year. Frankfurt-listed shares fell about 3% in evening trade after the announcement, according to Reuters.

BMW said its redundancy programme was moving faster than planned, which will bring larger severance payments in the fourth quarter. The company said it would use that momentum to accelerate a wider overhaul of its organisation and processes, including cutting management roles more quickly than previously announced. Earlier plans had included about 8,000 job cuts.

Part of the pressure reflects stronger demand. BMW said sales of new models built on its Neue Klasse platform were running high enough to require extra production shifts, adding costs in the near term.

Even so, the company now expects deliveries to fall more steeply this year than it had anticipated. Reuters reported the decline in automotive deliveries at between 5% and 9.9%. BMW, whose brands include Mini and Rolls-Royce, delivered about 2.5 million vehicles last year.

The company still expects automotive free cash flow above €2.5bn, which suggests the cut reflects one-off charges more than a collapse in underlying cash generation.

China remains the central challenge. Like its German rivals, BMW faces fierce competition and falling demand in the world’s largest car market, where buyers are increasingly turning to cheaper local brands. Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen have also issued profit warnings this year and are cutting jobs to reduce costs.

BMW reports third-quarter results on Wednesday, when investors will look for detail on the size of the restructuring charges and any sign that demand in China is stabilising. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Central bank gold buying jumps 42% in Q3 as high prices hit jewellery demand, WGC says
item.description:
The split in demand matters for price support: central banks tend to buy steadily rather than chase prices, so their stepped-up purchases act as a floor under gold in a way retail demand cannot. The weakness in jewellery and bar and coin buying shows gold’s rally has relied more on institutional and official money than on households, leaving it more exposed if fund inflows reverse. The near-collapse in recycling at these prices is notable, as owners appear to be holding gold rather than selling, which tightens available supply. Investors should weigh the council’s upbeat outlook against its position as an industry body funded by producers.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold trims gains after overnight strikes on Iran as the focus turns to the US midterm elections

--- Central banks are buying gold faster than ever while households balk at the price, and that split is now doing much of the work holding up demand.

Summary:

  • Central banks bought about 320 tonnes in Q3, up 42% on the year, and around 675 tonnes so far in 2026
  • Total demand was about 1,370 tonnes, down 1%, with year-to-date demand level with 2025’s record
  • Jewellery consumption fell 17% to the weakest third quarter in the series, though spending rose 2%
  • Bar and coin demand fell 19%, while ETFs took in about 210 tonnes
  • Mine output hit a Q3 record, while recycling fell to a three-year low
  • Gold averaged around $4,260/oz, up 23% on the year

Central banks stepped up their gold purchases sharply in the third quarter, offsetting a slump in jewellery and retail investment demand as high prices weighed on consumers, according to the World Gold Council.

The industry body, which is funded by gold miners, published its quarterly Gold Demand Trends report. It estimated that central banks bought about 320 tonnes in the three months to September, up 42% from a year earlier. That took their purchases for the year so far to around 675 tonnes, 6% above the same period of 2025.

Total demand, including over-the-counter trading, was roughly 1,370 tonnes, down 1% on the year. Year-to-date demand of about 3,880 tonnes is level with 2025’s record pace, and its value reached a record of around $566bn. Gold averaged around $4,260 an ounce in the quarter, up 23% on the year and the third-highest quarterly average on record.

High prices took their toll on price-sensitive buyers. Jewellery consumption fell 17% to about 310 tonnes, the weakest third quarter in the council’s data series. Spending on jewellery still rose 2% to around $43bn, as buyers paid more for less metal. Demand for bars and coins dropped 19% to about 270 tonnes.

Exchange-traded funds provided some support, taking in about 210 tonnes and reversing outflows in the second quarter, though inflows were 6% lower than a year earlier. Overall investment demand, combining funds, bars and coins, fell 14%.

On the supply side, mine production rose 3% to a third-quarter record of about 1,070 tonnes, while recycling fell 8% to a three-year low. The council said recycling has stayed largely unresponsive to high prices. Technology demand rose 3%, helped by AI-related electronics manufacturing.

Looking ahead, the council expects central bank buying for 2026 to at least match last year’s level. It sees investment demand remaining resilient, jewellery volumes continuing to soften, and only modest growth in supply, coming mainly from mines.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US warns of Houthi threat to Saudi airports and infrastructure, curbs travel to oil areas
item.description:
For oil, the alert matters less for what has happened than for where Washington now sees risk. By naming Qatif and Yanbu, it points to the possibility of strikes on processing and export infrastructure, not just airports. That threat could support a geopolitical risk premium in Brent even without physical disruption. Yanbu is especially sensitive because it is Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route if Gulf shipping is threatened, so any attack there would hit a key buffer for global supply. The wider risk-off backdrop could also lift demand for haven assets, while Gulf equities and airline stocks remain exposed to further disruption.

---

Washington’s latest Saudi alert reports no new strike, but it names the kingdom’s oil heartland and its back-up export route as places its own staff should stay away from.

Summary:

  • The US Mission to Saudi Arabia updated its security alert on 3 November, covering the whole country
  • It says Houthi attacks have hit civilian airports and critical infrastructure, causing casualties and severe travel disruption
  • It warns hostilities could escalate rapidly beyond the immediate area
  • US staff need special authorisation to travel to Qatif, Yanbu, Jizan, Asir, Najran and Taif, and may not go within 20 miles of the Yemen border
  • Non-emergency US staff were ordered to leave Saudi Arabia on 23 October
  • Riyadh airport has partially reopened, while Jeddah and Dammam airports face delays and cancellations

The United States has updated its security alert for Saudi Arabia, warning of possible further attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi forces on airports and critical infrastructure. It has also restricted travel by its staff to areas that include the kingdom’s main oil-producing and export regions.

According to the alert issued by the US Mission to Saudi Arabia on 3 November, the Houthis have attacked the kingdom, including civilian airports and critical infrastructure, causing civilian casualties and severe travel disruption. The mission warned that the hostilities could escalate rapidly beyond the immediate area. It told US citizens to expect possible attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and wider travel disruption.

US government personnel now need special authorisation to travel to several locations. These include Qatif in the Eastern Province and Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, as well as Jizan, Asir, Najran and Taif. Staff are barred from travelling within 20 miles of the Yemen border and need approval to use any Saudi airport.

The alert does not appear to describe a new attack. The State Department ordered non-emergency staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia on 23 October. Houthi missile and drone strikes on Saudi airports date back to at least early October, including a deadly attack on Riyadh airport. Riyadh airport has since partially reopened, while airports in Jeddah and Dammam are operating with some delays and cancellations.

The locations named in the travel restrictions are what make the update significant for energy markets. Qatif sits close to some of the world’s most important oil processing and export facilities. Yanbu is the kingdom’s main Red Sea outlet, a route that allows Saudi crude to bypass the Gulf when shipping there is at risk. Naming both areas, alongside references to attacks on critical infrastructure, signals that Washington sees a credible threat to sites well beyond the airports targeted so far.

Saudi authorities have also warned that sharing images or information about missile and drone interceptions or impact sites can lead to legal action. That may limit how quickly details of any future strikes become public. 

Yanbu is home of Red Sea export infrastructure

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Carney says US trade talks to intensify as Washington asks less and offers mor
item.description:
Carney’s remarks offer modest support for the Canadian dollar, as any easing of the 50% US tariff would lift a weight on Canadian exporters and the growth outlook. The lack of a timeline limits how much a trade-deal premium can build, so USD/CAD is likely to stay more sensitive to the US midterm results and oil prices in the near term. Canada is the largest foreign supplier of crude to the US, so a broader settlement would also reduce one source of uncertainty for North American energy flows. Sectors hit by Canada’s counter-tariffs, including US steel, dairy and farm equipment exporters, stand to gain most if talks succeed.

-

Carney is sounding more optimistic about a US trade deal than at any point since talks collapsed in August, but he is careful not to promise one.

Summary:

  • Carney said trade discussions with the US will become more intensive
  • He said some red lines had been removed but others still need to be addressed
  • The US is asking for less and offering more, he said, but the two sides are not there yet
  • He said direct talks between negotiators and the USTR are not always needed because good communication channels are open
  • The US imposed a 50% tariff on about $20bn of Canadian goods after talks broke down in August, and Canada retaliated
  • The comments come as Americans vote in midterm elections

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade discussions with the United States will become more intensive. He reported progress in the talks while cautioning that important areas remain unresolved and a deal is not yet done.

Carney said some of the red lines in the negotiations had been removed, but others still needed to be addressed. He described the shift in Washington’s position as the United States asking for less and offering more, while stressing that the two sides were not there yet.

He also played down the need for formal negotiating rounds. He said it was not always necessary for Canadian trade negotiators to be talking directly with the Office of the US Trade Representative, because good lines of communication were open between the two governments.

The comments build on Carney’s update over the weekend, when he said he had held a good conversation with President Donald Trump. He said then that teams from both countries would work over the coming weeks on the outlines of a deal. Trump said last week that he expected a new agreement pretty soon, without giving details.

The talks are trying to repair a relationship that deteriorated sharply in August, when negotiations broke down. Trump then imposed a 50% tariff on around $20bn of Canadian goods, equal to roughly 5.5% of Canada’s exports. Ottawa responded with matching tariffs on US products including steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

Carney’s tone is notably more upbeat than at any point since that breakdown, but his remarks were careful to avoid suggesting an agreement was imminent. His repeated references to unresolved areas and remaining red lines suggest the hardest issues are still on the table, and he gave no timeline for a final deal.

The timing adds a political dimension. Americans vote in midterm elections on Tuesday, and trade tensions with Canada are a live issue in states such as Michigan and Maine. The outcome could shape how much room the White House has to compromise in the weeks ahead. 

The two will cross paths at the APEC Summit in China, in Shenzhen from November 17 to 18

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZ Q3 Unemployment rate 5.7% (expected 5.5%, prior 5.6%)
item.description:
The miss on every major measure is likely to weigh on the New Zealand dollar and trim pricing for a December rate hike. The kiwi was already near a cycle low against the Australian dollar after last week’s RBNZ hold, and the gap with a more hawkish RBA now looks set to widen. The weak jobs figures argue against tightening, but the RBNZ’s hawks have focused on core inflation and fuel costs. A labour market miss alone may not settle the debate, so inflation expectations surveys later this month carry extra weight. Front-end swap rates are the market to watch for how far hike bets are pared.

--- Banks called the peak in New Zealand unemployment, but the labour market went the other way, and the RBNZ’s December hike now looks a harder sell.

Summary:

  • Unemployment rose to 5.7% in Q3 from 5.6%, against a Reuters poll forecast of 5.5%
  • Employment fell 0.1% on the quarter, against expectations of a 0.4% gain, and Q2 growth was revised down to 0.3%
  • The participation rate dropped to 70.4% from 70.6%, below the 70.7% forecast
  • Private sector wages excluding overtime rose 0.4% on the quarter and 2.0% on the year, both slightly below forecasts
  • The RBNZ held rates at 2.75% last week on a 4:3 vote, with the next decision on 9 December
  • New Zealand holds a general election on Saturday

New Zealand’s unemployment rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, above expectations of 5.5%, as employment unexpectedly fell and wage growth slowed, data from Statistics New Zealand showed on Wednesday.

Employment declined 0.1% from the previous quarter, against a Reuters poll forecast of a 0.4% gain. The participation rate dropped to 70.4% from 70.6%, below the 70.7% expected. Unemployment rose even though fewer people were looking for work, which points to weak hiring rather than a growing labour force. Earlier figures were also revised lower, with second-quarter employment growth cut to 0.3% from 0.5%.

The result runs against bank forecasts that had pointed to a peak in joblessness. Westpac had expected the rate to ease to 5.5%, while ANZ had forecast no change at 5.6%. The June quarter reading of 5.6% was already the highest since 2015.

Wage pressures also eased. Private sector wages excluding overtime rose 0.4% in the quarter, below the 0.5% expected, taking annual growth to 2.0% from 2.1%.

The data lands at a sensitive moment for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. On 28 October it held the official cash rate at 2.75% in a 4:3 vote, surprising markets that had largely priced a hike. The majority cited weaker than expected inflation, stable inflation expectations and subdued wage growth, and argued that two earlier rate increases needed time to work. Wednesday’s figures support that case on both jobs and pay.

Westpac had described today’s release as the first key input before the RBNZ’s next decision on 9 December, while still forecasting a hike at that meeting. The bank cautioned that the move was not a done deal, and a weaker labour market makes that case harder to argue.

New Zealand holds a general election on Saturday, adding further uncertainty to the policy outlook ahead of the December meeting. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq rebounds as chip stocks rally and Dow slips
item.description:
U.S. stocks closed mixed on Tuesday. The Nasdaq Composite led the rebound with a 0.83% gain, and the Nasdaq 100 added 0.68%. The S&P 500 and Russell 2000 also finished higher, while the Dow fell 197 points. Chip stocks helped lead the move, with Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom all gaining more than 2%.

The S&P 500’s close told only part of the story. Decliners outnumbered advancers 318 to 167 in the index, and only nine of the Dow’s 30 stocks finished higher. Nasdaq breadth was positive, with 1,630 advancers against 1,566 decliners. Buyers made more progress in tech, but participation was still fairly narrow.

U.S. closing levels

  • Dow Industrial Average −197.00 points (−0.38%) to 51,792.19
  • S&P 500 +27.52 points (+0.36%) to 7,568.92
  • Nasdaq Composite +207.69 points (+0.83%) to 25,372.01
  • Russell 2000 +6.57 points (+0.23%) to 2,812.45
  • Nasdaq 100 +190.44 points (+0.68%) to 28,180.26

Chip stocks lead, while Apple bucks the move

  • Microsoft rose 2.74%, Meta gained 2.36%, Nvidia added 2.27% and Amazon rose 2.06%. Alphabet edged up 0.37%, while Apple fell 1.90%.
  • Credo gained 7.78%, Monolithic Power Systems rose 6.78% and SanDisk added 4.78%. AMD closed up 3.65% at $483.90 heading into its earnings release, while Texas Instruments rose 3.46% and Broadcom gained 3.07%.
  • Outside the chip names, Bloom Energy rose 9.05%, AppLovin gained 7.28%, Nebius added 7.25% and GE Vernova climbed 6.49%.

Nasdaq buyers keep the 200-day moving averages in play

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,372.01 after Monday’s selloff took it to 25,145.95, just above its rising 200-day moving average near 25,073. The buyers have some room off that support now. On a pullback, Monday’s low is the first barometer. A move below it would put the 200-day back in focus, and getting and staying below the average would increase the bearish bias.

The Nasdaq 100 came even closer to its 200-day moving average on Monday, bottoming at 27,967.44 against the average near 27,952.83. Tuesday’s close at 28,180.26 gives buyers some breathing room. The next test on the topside is near 28,538. Getting and staying above that level would have traders looking toward the 28,822–28,953 swing area.

Trading lesson

Pair the index close with the advance-decline count. In a capitalization-weighted index like the S&P 500, gains in a few large stocks can lift the index even as most members fall. If the index extends its rebound and more stocks join in, that tells you buyers are gaining ground across more of the market. Tuesday’s S&P 500 close leaves that as a question for the next session.

After the close, AMD and Super Micro beat on earnings and revenue

All seven companies topped adjusted EPS estimates, and six beat on revenue. Super Micro Computer posted the largest revenue beat of the group, coming in $3.88 billion above expectations. AMD beat by $0.14 per share and $300 million in revenue. Booking Holdings was the lone revenue miss, coming in $650 million below expectations even as earnings beat.

  • Block — Adj. EPS $1.13 vs. $1.03 (BEAT) · Revenue $6.72B vs. $6.58B (BEAT). Shares are trading at $82.10 up 8.03%. The price is back above its 100 day moving average at $78.24

  • Booking Holdings — Adj. EPS $4.66 vs. $4.49 (BEAT) · Revenue $8.90B vs. $9.55B (MISS). It's shares are trading down 2.26% at $152.82. The price is moving away from its 100 hour moving average at $156.60, and its 200 hour moving average at $158.17.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, November 4, 2026 - NZ jobs report, China PMI
item.description:
The RatingDog PMI data follows official and their manufacturing PMIs earlier this week:

  • details on these in the wrap for Monday, investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Oil eases on Doha talks

The NZ Q3 labour market data is due at 10:45am New Zealand time. 

What’s expected

Forecasts range from 5.4% to 5.6%. The June quarter’s 5.6% was the highest since September 2015. Westpac expects employment to rise 0.5% and the rate to slip to 5.5%. ANZ expects employment up 0.3% and the rate unchanged at 5.6%. ANZ’s flat call rests on a rise in labour force participation absorbing the job gains. The RBNZ’s September forecast was 5.5%. Wage growth is expected to stay modest. Private-sector labour cost growth is forecast at around 2.1%, which economists describe as near a four-year low.

RBNZ implications

The RBNZ surprised markets on October 28 by holding the OCR at 2.75% on a 4:3 vote, when a 25bp hike had been almost fully priced. The majority pointed to softer than expected Q3 inflation, stable inflation expectations and subdued wage growth. That makes today’s wage figures especially relevant. Westpac still expects a hike on December 9 but says it is not a done deal, and lists today’s data as the first key input. ANZ also still forecasts a December move.

NZD implications

After the hold, AUD/NZD jumped to a cycle high around 1.26, with interest rate differentials weighing on the kiwi as the RBA turned more hawkish.

  • Hawkish case: a drop in unemployment to 5.4% or 5.5% plus firmer wages would likely revive December hike pricing and give the kiwi some relief.
  • Dovish case: an unchanged 5.6% with soft wages would support the doves on the committee and leave the NZD vulnerable.

Participation is the swing factor. A rise could hold the headline rate steady even if jobs are growing.

There is also an election on Saturday, November 7. Policy expectations could shift if a Labour-led government looks likely, given its stated aim to restore the RBNZ’s dual mandate.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AMD shares rise after hours as Q4 revenue outlook of $17bn tops forecasts on AI ramp
item.description:
AMD’s guide adds to a strong evening for the AI hardware trade, landing alongside Super Micro’s beat and raised outlook, which may support chip and server names in the next session. The size of the fourth-quarter step-up will sharpen the comparison with Nvidia, since AMD is pitching Helios as a direct rack-scale rival. The slightly lower margin guide is unlikely to spoil the reaction on its own. It is still a reminder that volume growth in AI accelerators may come at some cost to profitability, which investors will weigh as the ramp scales.

---

AMD beat modestly on the quarter but promised a big jump in the next one, betting that its Helios AI racks can turn into the growth engine investors have been waiting for.

Summary:

  • Q3 revenue was around $13.4bn, ahead of the roughly $13.1bn expected and up about 53% from a year earlier
  • Adjusted EPS was about $2.10, against forecasts near $1.95
  • Adjusted operating margin was 29%, against expectations of 28%, with adjusted gross margin of 56%
  • Q4 revenue guidance is around $17bn, above expectations of about $16.3bn
  • Q4 adjusted gross margin guidance is 55%, slightly below the 55.5% expected
  • AMD expects growth to accelerate as Helios and Venice production scales
  • Shares rose in after-hours trade

Advanced Micro Devices shares rose in after-hours trade after the chipmaker beat third-quarter forecasts and guided fourth-quarter revenue well above expectations. It said growth should accelerate further as it ramps production of its Helios AI rack system and next-generation Venice server processors.

According to the company’s results, revenue came in at around $13.4bn, ahead of expectations of about $13.1bn and above the roughly $13bn midpoint of its own guidance. That compares with about $8.8bn a year earlier, a gain of roughly 53%. Adjusted earnings per share were about $2.10, against forecasts near $1.95. Adjusted net income reached around $3.5bn, compared with expectations of about $3.2bn.

Profitability also edged ahead of forecasts. Adjusted operating income was around $3.9bn, above the roughly $3.7bn expected, giving an adjusted operating margin of 29% against forecasts of 28%. On a reported basis, operating income was about $2.8bn. Adjusted gross margin was 56%, in line with the company’s guidance, while the reported gross margin was 54%. Capital spending of around $650m was in line with expectations.

The outlook is the headline. AMD expects fourth-quarter revenue of around $17bn, against expectations of about $16.3bn. That would mark a rise of roughly 27% from the third quarter, a sharp step-up for a company of its size. Helios is AMD’s rack-scale AI platform built around its MI450 accelerators. Management has previously described Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic as anchor customers for multi-gigawatt deployments.

The one softer detail is margin. AMD guided fourth-quarter adjusted gross margin to 55%, slightly below expectations of 55.5% and a touch lower than the third quarter. Analysts had flagged that AI accelerators carry lower margins than the company average, so a faster Helios ramp may dilute gross margin even as revenue climbs.

Investors will look to the earnings call for detail on the pace of the Helios ramp, on supply constraints in memory and advanced packaging, and on visibility into AI demand for 2027. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Super Micro shares rise after hours as revenue nears $20bn and Q2 guidance tops forecasts
item.description:
The after-hours gain extends a rally that began with last month’s preliminary update, and the strong current-quarter guide gives the AI hardware trade another demand signal. In October, rival server makers Dell and HPE rallied in sympathy, so a similar read-through is possible in the next session. The full-year range is the weak point: it sits only modestly above expectations and could cap enthusiasm once investors work through the second-half arithmetic. The customer mix and margins remain the swing factors for whether the rally holds.

---

Super Micro cleared even the higher bar it set for itself last month, though its full-year forecast quietly assumes the pace slows.

Summary:

  • Q1 revenue was around $19.9bn, against expectations of about $16bn and above the company’s own preliminary range of $18.5bn to $19.5bn
  • Adjusted EPS was roughly $1.80, ahead of forecasts near $1.20
  • Q2 revenue guidance is $19.5bn to $21.5bn, above the roughly $18bn expected
  • Q2 adjusted EPS guidance is $1.66 to $1.90, against forecasts near $1.14
  • Full-year revenue guidance is $72bn to $78bn, broadly in line with expectations around $73bn
  • Shares rose in after-hours trade

Super Micro Computer shares rose in after-hours trade after the AI server maker reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of nearly $20bn. It also guided the current quarter higher still, extending the run of growth it previewed in a surprise update last month.

According to the company’s results, revenue for the September quarter came in at around $19.9bn, against analyst expectations of about $16bn. Adjusted earnings per share were roughly $1.80, well ahead of forecasts near $1.20.

The consensus figures overstate the size of the surprise. On 20 October, Super Micro said it expected first-quarter revenue of $18.5bn to $19.5bn, far above its earlier guidance of $14.5bn to $15.5bn, and its shares jumped 14% in extended trade on the news. Many published estimates do not appear to have caught up with that update. Even so, the final revenue figure landed above the top end of the company’s own preliminary range.

The outlook is the stronger signal. Super Micro expects second-quarter revenue of $19.5bn to $21.5bn, against expectations of about $18bn. It expects adjusted earnings per share of $1.66 to $1.90, compared with forecasts near $1.14. For the full fiscal year, it sees revenue of $72bn to $78bn, broadly in line with expectations of around $73bn.

That full-year range carries an implication worth noting. The first-quarter result and the midpoint of second-quarter guidance add up to roughly $40bn for the first half. The midpoint of the annual forecast would then leave about $35bn for the second half, or close to $17bn a quarter, below the pace of the first two quarters. Management may simply be guiding conservatively, but the arithmetic suggests the company is not assuming the current run-rate continues all year.

Questions raised after the October update remain open. One is how much of the business comes from the largest cloud providers compared with newer AI-focused cloud companies. Another is whether the margin improvement flagged last month has held. Investors will look to the company’s earnings call for answers on both. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Two reasons why the US could attack Iran as soon as tomorrow
item.description:
Oil has been falling this week but there's a fair argument that Trump could be attempting to send false signals in order to lower oil prices ahead of the vote. 

Behind the scenes, the US military has been angling to be in a position to attack immediately after the midterms. The New York Times cites US officials who say the US military could resume major combat operations against Iran as early as Wednesday.

There are two reasons they US could launch the type of short and intense campaign Trump has teased. The first is that there are currently three US aircraft carriers in the region but one must return home in early November.

  • USS George H.W. Bush— Already operating in the region.

  • USS George Washington — Redeployed from the Pacific to the Middle East.

  • USS Theodore Roosevelt — Deployed from San Diego in late September to reinforce U.S. forces.

The USS George Washington is likely the one that needs to leave, returning ot its normal operating area near Japan.

Secondly, early November is also a period of moonless nights and that's the darkness the US military generally prefers for its attacks, the report says.

The NYT writes:

U.S. Central Command has a plan to strike Iran beginning as early as Wednesday, after the U.S. midterm elections and when three aircraft carriers are in the region, according to U.S. officials.
The ideal conditions for the type of campaign the military has laid out will last only a short time. After early November, one of the aircraft carriers will need to return to its home port. Early November is also a period of moonless nights, the kind of deep darkness the U.S. military likes to use for its attacks.

In any case, Wednesday should be a volatile day.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Booking Holdings shares slide as Q3 revenue misses despite earnings and bookings beat
item.description:
The after-hours selling suggests investors care more about how much revenue Booking earns from its bookings than about volume. Strong gross bookings did not make up for the shortfall. The miss lands on a stock already down about 30% this year, which leaves little room for disappointment and could weigh on online travel peers in early trade. Oil is part of the backdrop: the company has linked higher flight prices and weaker long-haul demand to the Middle East conflict, so energy-driven airfare costs remain a risk to travel revenue.

---

Booking’s customers booked more travel than expected, but less of it turned into revenue, and that gap is what investors sold.

Summary:

  • Q3 revenue was around $8.9bn, short of expectations near $9.6bn
  • Adjusted EPS was about $4.70, ahead of forecasts near $4.50
  • Gross bookings were roughly $54.5bn, above estimates of about $52.7bn
  • Shares fell in after-hours trade
  • Management had guided Q3 revenue growth of 4% to 6%, citing Middle East conflict effects on flights and long-haul travel
  • Per-share figures reflect April’s 25-for-1 stock split

Booking Holdings shares fell in after-hours trade after the online travel group reported third-quarter revenue well short of expectations, overshadowing a beat on both adjusted earnings and gross bookings.

According to the company’s earnings release, revenue came in at around $8.9bn, against analyst expectations of about $9.6bn. Adjusted earnings per share were roughly $4.70, ahead of forecasts near $4.50. Gross bookings, which measure the total value of travel booked through the group’s platforms, reached around $54.5bn and topped estimates of about $52.7bn.

The mix of results points to a widening gap between activity on the platform and the revenue the company keeps from it. Customers booked more travel than expected, but less of that value turned into revenue than analysts had modelled. The shortfall also appears to fall outside the company’s own guidance. Management had guided third-quarter revenue growth of 4% to 6%. Figures cited ahead of the release put the year-earlier quarter at roughly $9bn, which suggests reported revenue was little changed or slightly lower.

The company had flagged a difficult quarter in advance. When it set its outlook in early August, management said it expected the indirect effects of the Middle East conflict to persist through the third quarter. Those effects included higher flight ticket prices, reduced capacity on some routes and softer demand for long-haul international travel, while domestic travel held up better. Currency moves were also expected to trim reported growth by about one percentage point.

The earnings figures reflect the 25-for-1 stock split that took effect in April, which explains why the per-share numbers are much smaller than in past years.

Attention now turns to the company’s conference call and fourth-quarter outlook. Investors will be looking for an explanation of the revenue shortfall and an update on how the conflict is affecting bookings. They will also want to know whether management still expects full-year revenue growth in the high single digits. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
